facts.fact_text: On 5 March 2012 the applicant took part in a meeting at Pushkinskaya Square, Moscow.
The meeting at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 had been called to protest against the allegedly rigged presidential elections in Russia.
The meeting at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 had been approved by the municipal authorities.
According to the applicant, those remaining at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 remained peacefully within the pedestrian area of the square and did not obstruct the traffic or access.
On 8 May 2012 the applicant took part in an overnight 'walkabout', an informal gathering whereby activists peacefully met at a public venue to discuss current affairs.
On 8 May 2012 several dozen activists met up to discuss the inauguration of Mr Vladimir Putin as President of Russia on the previous day (7 May 2012).
At 4.30 a.m. on 8 May 2012, according to the applicant, the applicant was walking down Lubyanskiy Proyezd accompanied by about 170 people.
On 8 May 2012 the group walking down Lubyanskiy Proyezd stopped on the stairs of a public building for a group photograph.
According to the applicant, the group walking down Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street on 8 May 2012 stayed on the pavement, had no banners or sound equipment, and were causing no nuisance.
On 9 May 2012 the applicant arrived at 5 a.m. at Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow to take part in an informal meeting with a State Duma deputy.
On 9 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow to attend the Victory Day celebrations.
On 9 May 2012 at Kudrinskaya Square the applicant was among 50 to 100 people peacefully 'walking about' and discussing current affairs.
According to the applicant, the gathering at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 was not a demonstration: there had been no banners and no noise, and no one was chanting slogans or giving speeches.
On 27 October 2012 the applicant held a static demonstration ('picket', пикетирование) at Lubyanskaya Square in Moscow.

The static demonstration at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 October 2012 was part of a series of peaceful pickets held in Moscow in front of the buildings housing the Federal Security Service and the Russian Investigation Committee to protest 'against repressions and torture'.

According to the applicant, his demonstration at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 October 2012 was a solo picket (одиночное пикетирование) which was not subject to a prior notification to the competent public authority.
In total, about thirty people consecutively took part in the picket event at Lubyanskaya Square on 27 October 2012.

According to the applicant, at the moment of his arrest on 27 October 2012 he had finished picketing and was peacefully walking along the pavement; he was not chanting or carrying any banners, but was being followed by a group of people, including journalists, whose number he estimated as 'two dozen'.

On 24 February 2014 at 12 noon the applicant went to the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow to attend a hearing involving activists who were on trial for participation in mass disorders at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow on 6 May 2012.
On 24 February 2014 the applicant remained outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow among other members of the public wishing to attend the hearing.

According to the applicant, on 24 February 2014 he was standing silently outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow when the police suddenly rushed into the crowd and arrested him, without any order, warning or pretext.
At about 7.45 p.m. on 24 February 2014 the applicant took part in a peaceful public gathering following the delivery of the judgment in respect of mass disorders at Bolotnaya Square.
The gathering on 24 February 2014 at about 7.45 p.m. had about 150 participants and took place at Tverskaya Street.
On 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street the applicant was arrested while he was standing on the pavement talking to a journalist.
According to the applicant, he had received no order or warning before his second arrest on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street, and he did not resist the police.
At 10.45 p.m. on 5 March 2012 the police arrived at Pushkinskaya Square and arrested the applicant, among many others.
After his arrest on 5 March 2012, the applicant was taken to the Tverskoy District police station.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events of 5 March 2012.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District fined the applicant RUB 1,000 (equivalent at the material time to about EUR 25) under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
On 8 May 2012, while the applicant was taking a group photograph on the stairs of a public building on Lubyanskiy Proyezd, he was arrested by riot police.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events at Lubyanskiy Proyezd on 8 May 2012.
On 8 May 2012 on Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street the group was surrounded by riot police and the applicant was arrested without any order or warning.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 (2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events at Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street on 8 May 2012.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District fined the applicant RUB 1,000 under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation in connection with the events at Lubyanskiy Proyezd on 8 May 2012.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 380 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow fined the applicant RUB 1,000 under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation in connection with the Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street incident.
At 6 a.m. on 9 May 2012 riot police arrived at Kudrinskaya Square and arrested the applicant without issuing any orders or warning.

The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative imprisonment by the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow in connection with the events at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012.
At 3.30 p.m. on 27 October 2012 the police arrested the applicant at 9 Maroseyka Street when he was walking down the street accompanied by a group of people.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events of 27 October 2012.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District fined the applicant RUB 30,000 (equivalent at the material time to about EUR 740) under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation in connection with the events of 27 October 2012.

According to the applicant, on 24 February 2014 he was standing silently outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow when the police suddenly rushed into the crowd and arrested him, without any order, warning or pretext.

The applicant was charged with a breach of the established procedure for conducting public events, an offence under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014.
On 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street the applicant was arrested while he was standing on the pavement talking to a journalist.

The applicant was charged with disobeying a lawful order of the police, an offence under Article 19 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation, in connection with the events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.
The applicant was sentenced to seven days' administrative imprisonment by the Tverskoy District Court in connection with the events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court fined the applicant RUB 10,000 (equivalent to about EUR 200) under Article 20 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation in connection with the events outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014.

The Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. 54-FZ of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), Section 2, defines a public event as an open, peaceful action accessible to all, held in the form of a gathering, a meeting, a demonstration, a march, or a picket or in various combinations of these forms, organised at the initiative of citizens of the Russian Federation, political parties, other public associations, or religious associations, including events held with the use of vehicles.

The Public Events Act, Section 2, provides that the aim of a public event is the free expression and formation of opinions, and to put forward demands on issues of political, economic, social and cultural life in the country, as well as issues of foreign policy.

The Public Events Act, Section 3, provides that a public event is based on the principle of legality, meaning compliance with the provisions of the Russian Constitution, the Public Events Act, and other legislative acts of the Russian Federation.

The Public Events Act, Section 5 § 4, provides that the organiser of a public event must notify the executive or municipal authority of the public event in accordance with Section 7 of the Public Events Act.

The Public Events Act, Section 7, provides that notification of a public event (except for a gathering and a picket held by a solo participant) must be filed in writing by its organiser with the executive or municipal authority no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days before the date of the public event.

The Public Events Act, Section 16, provides that the grounds for ending a public event include: the emergence of a genuine threat to citizens' lives or health, and to the possessions of physical or legal persons; commission by the participants of unlawful acts or a deliberate breach by the organiser of the requirements on the procedure for the conduct of public events; and (following legislative amendments of 8 June 2012) non-compliance by the organisers with the obligations set out in Section 5 § 4 of the Public Events Act.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 1, provides that if it is decided to end the public event, the representative of the executive or municipal authority shall give an order to the organiser to end the public event, having explained the reasons for its termination, and within twenty-four hours shall issue this order in writing and serve it on the organiser; shall set the time for compliance with the order; and if the organiser does not comply, shall directly address the participants and set an additional time for compliance.
The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 2, provides that in the event of non-compliance with the order to end the public event, the police shall take the necessary measures to end the public event.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 3, provides that the procedure for ending a public event set out in Section 17 § 1 shall not apply in the event of mass disorder, mob violence, arson, or other situations requiring urgent action.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 4, provides that failure to obey lawful orders from police officers or resistance to them by certain participants of the public event may incur liability as provided for by law.

Prior to 8 June 2012, Article 19 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative imprisonment of up to fifteen days.

Prior to 8 June 2012, Article 20 § 2 (1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage, payable by the organisers.

Prior to 8 June 2012, Article 20 § 2 (2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between RUB 1,000 and RUB 2,000 for the organisers, and between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 for the participants.
On 8 June 2012 the Code of Administrative Offences was amended by Law no. 65-FZ.

Following the amendments of 8 June 2012 (Law no. 65-FZ), a breach of the procedure for organising or running a public event by an organiser became punishable by a fine of between RUB 10,000 and RUB 20,000 or up to forty hours of community work under Article 20 § 2 (1) of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Following the amendments of 8 June 2012 (Law no. 65-FZ), the organisation or running of a public event without notifying the competent public authority became punishable by a fine of between RUB 20,000 and RUB 30,000 or up to fifty hours of community work under Article 20 § 2 (2) of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Following the amendments of 8 June 2012 (Law no. 65-FZ), stricter penalties were introduced under Article 20 § 2 (3 and 4) of the Code of Administrative Offences for the above actions or inaction where they obstructed pedestrians or traffic, or caused damage to health or property.

Following the amendments of 8 June 2012 (Law no. 65-FZ), separate offences were introduced under Article 20 § 2 (5) and (6) of the Code of Administrative Offences concerning violations by an event participant of the procedure for running the event, and where such violations caused damage to health or property.

Following the amendments of 8 June 2012 (Law no. 65-FZ), Article 4.5 of the Code of Administrative Offences was amended to increase the limitation period for the offence under Article 20 § 2 from two months to one year.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 stated that ensuring the safety of participants and public order is a legitimate consideration, but this should not translate into a lack of tolerance towards peaceful public events which have not been agreed with the authorities.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 stated that the 2012 amendments to the Russian legislation on assemblies gave broad grounds for the dispersal of public events, including any irregularities in the organisation or the conduct of public events, some of which are not clearly defined in law.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 noted that one of the concerns about the 2012 amendments expressed by the Presidential Council was the lack of clarity in terms of which actions or omissions can trigger administrative liability.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 noted that earlier clarifications by the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation that there must be compelling public order considerations to make holding a public event impossible seem to have had little effect in practice.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 reported a growing intolerance towards unauthorised public events involving relatively low numbers of peaceful participants, including even single-person pickets which are formally exempt from the agreement procedure.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 stated that the need to maintain public order should not be interpreted in such a way as to strip the right to freedom of peaceful assembly of its meaning.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 stated that according to international standards, if the domestic legal framework foresees a notification procedure, its objective should be to allow State authorities the opportunity to facilitate the exercise of the right to freedom of assembly, and that failure to notify the authorities of an assembly does not render it unlawful and should not be used as a basis for dispersing it.

Article 55 § 3 of the Russian Constitution provides that the rights and freedoms of individuals and citizens may be limited by federal law only to the extent required for the protection of the fundamental principles of the constitutional system, morality, health, the rights and lawful interests of other people, and for ensuring the defence of the country and the security of the State.

The Public Events Act, Section 17 § 2, provides that in the event of non-compliance with the order to end the public event, the police shall take the necessary measures to end the public event.
According to the applicant, those remaining at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 remained peacefully within the pedestrian area of the square and did not obstruct the traffic or access.
According to the Government, the applicant was holding an irregular gathering at Pushkinskaya Square on 5 March 2012 without prior notification and was shouting political slogans.
On the evening of 5 March 2012 two policemen drew up a report on the administrative offence stating that the applicant had been arrested at 10.45 p.m. 'in a fountain' at Pushkinskaya Square.
The administrative offence report drawn up on 5 March 2012 stated that the applicant had taken part in an irregular public gathering.
The administrative offence report drawn up on 5 March 2012 stated that the applicant had ignored police orders to disperse.

The applicant challenged the authenticity of the police reports and the witness statement of the two police officers on the grounds that he had been arrested by different police officers from those who drew up the reports.
The applicant's objection challenging the authenticity of the police reports and witness statements was dismissed by the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District.

On the basis of the written statements and testimony of two police officers, the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 369 of the Tverskoy District found the applicant guilty of taking part in an irregular public gathering conducted without prior notification.

The journalist eyewitness testified at the appeal hearing on 10 April 2012 that before being arrested the applicant was standing 'in a fountain, holding hands with others' and chanting political slogans.

The journalist eyewitness testified at the appeal hearing on 10 April 2012 that the police officers who had placed the applicant in the police bus were the same officers who had signed the report and who had appeared at the first-instance hearing.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow examined two video recordings submitted by the applicant at the appeal hearing on 10 April 2012.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow found at the appeal hearing on 10 April 2012 that State Duma deputy Mr P. had indeed called a public meeting.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow concluded at the appeal hearing on 10 April 2012 that at the time of his arrest the applicant was not meeting State Duma deputy Mr P. but was participating in a protest assembly.
According to the applicant, the group walking down Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street on 8 May 2012 stayed on the pavement, had no banners or sound equipment, and were causing no nuisance.
On 8 May 2012 on Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street the group was surrounded by riot police and the applicant was arrested without any order or warning.
The applicant's lawyer disputed the applicant's participation in an irregular assembly at Lubyanskiy Proyezd and claimed that the applicant had not chanted any slogans.
The applicant's lawyer asked the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District to admit video evidence and to examine certain eyewitnesses, but she refused to do so.

On the basis of written statements by two police officers, the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District found the applicant guilty of taking part in a meeting conducted before 7 a.m., in breach of regulations.

The police officer who arrested the applicant at Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street testified that he had arrested the applicant because the applicant was walking in a big group of people, obstructing traffic and chanting political slogans.
The eyewitnesses at the hearing on 1 June 2012 testified that the applicant had been walking down Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street with about fifty or sixty people.
The eyewitnesses at the hearing on 1 June 2012 testified that the police had blocked the group's way on Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street and had begun to arrest them without any warning.
The eyewitnesses at the hearing on 1 June 2012 denied hearing any slogans or amplified sound at Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 380 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow refused to admit video evidence in the proceedings concerning the Bolshaya Nikitskaya Street incident.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 380 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow dismissed the eyewitness statements on the grounds that the eyewitnesses were likely to be the applicant's supporters and were therefore biased.
According to the applicant, the gathering at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 was not a demonstration: there had been no banners and no noise, and no one was chanting slogans or giving speeches.
At 6 a.m. on 9 May 2012 riot police arrived at Kudrinskaya Square and arrested the applicant without issuing any orders or warning.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow refused the applicant's request that the police officers who had arrested him be called and examined.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow refused the applicant's request that video evidence be admitted.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow granted the applicant's request for examination of three eyewitnesses.

The three eyewitnesses at the hearing before the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow testified that there had been a public meeting with a State Duma deputy at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 to discuss current political developments.
The three eyewitnesses testified that no one at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 had chanted slogans or made noise or obstructed traffic.
The three eyewitnesses testified that the police had not issued any orders or warnings before arresting the applicant at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012.

On the basis of the written statements of two police officers, the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow established that the applicant had taken part in an irregular public meeting at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012 and had disobeyed a lawful order from the police to disperse.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow found that the applicant had chanted the slogans 'Russia without Putin!' and 'Putin is a thief!' at Kudrinskaya Square on 9 May 2012.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow found that the applicant had refused to leave Kudrinskaya Square, which needed to be cleared for the Victory Day celebrations.

The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 375 of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow rejected the statements of the three eyewitnesses on the grounds that they had given different estimates of the number of people present at Kudrinskaya Square, the number of police officers who arrested the applicant, and the time of his arrival at the meeting.

According to the applicant, at the moment of his arrest on 27 October 2012 he had finished picketing and was peacefully walking along the pavement; he was not chanting or carrying any banners, but was being followed by a group of people, including journalists, whose number he estimated as 'two dozen'.
According to the Government, the applicant had organised an irregular march on 27 October 2012 without prior notification.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District examined three eyewitnesses called at the applicant's request in the proceedings concerning the events of 27 October 2012.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District refused the applicant's request that the police officers who had arrested him on 27 October 2012 be called and examined.
The applicant's request that a video recording of the events of 27 October 2012 be admitted as evidence was refused by the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District.

The applicant's request that a written report from an NGO which had observed the pickets on 27 October 2012 be admitted in evidence was refused by the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District.

The three eyewitnesses examined at the applicant's request testified that after ending his picket on 27 October 2012, the applicant had walked down the street while speaking with a fellow activist, surrounded by journalists; he remained on the pavement, did not chant slogans, and carried no banners.
The three eyewitnesses testified that several other participants in the picket on 27 October 2012 remained standing with their banners, at a certain distance from each other.
The three eyewitnesses testified that the police arrested the applicant on 27 October 2012 without any warning or explanation.

On the basis of written reports by two police officers, the Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District established that the applicant had organised and led a group of thirty people on 27 October 2012, thus holding a march without the approval of the local authorities.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District established that the group on 27 October 2012 was heading from Lubyanskaya Square to Lefortovo detention facility.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District established that at 9 Maroseyka Street on 27 October 2012 the group had obstructed the road, thus halting traffic.
The Justice of the Peace of Circuit no. 387 of the Basmannyy District dismissed the witness statements in the applicant's favour on the grounds that they contradicted the evidence in the case file.

According to the applicant, on 24 February 2014 he was standing silently outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow when the police suddenly rushed into the crowd and arrested him, without any order, warning or pretext.
According to the official version, on 24 February 2014 outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow the applicant was holding an irregular gathering and chanting political slogans.
According to the applicant, he had received no order or warning before his second arrest on 24 February 2014 at Tverskaya Street, and he did not resist the police.

According to the police report, when the applicant was being seated in the police vehicle on 24 February 2014 he was waving at the crowd and trying to attract media attention, thus demonstrating a refusal to comply with the police order and resisting the officers in the performance of their duties.

The two eyewitnesses at the hearing on 25 February 2014 testified that the police had not given the applicant any orders or warnings before proceeding to arrest him at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.
The Tverskoy District Court admitted and examined the video recording of the contested events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014.
The Tverskoy District Court questioned the two police officers on whose reports the charges arising from the events at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014 were based.
The Tverskoy District Court established that the applicant had taken part in an irregular meeting at Tverskaya Street on 24 February 2014 and had disobeyed the lawful order of the police to disperse.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court dismissed the applicant's requests for examination of two eyewitnesses and two policemen at the hearing on 7 March 2014.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court admitted a video recording of the contested events outside the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow on 24 February 2014, but decided not to take cognisance of its contents because it was undated and because it had not reproduced the full sequence of events.

On the basis of the written reports by two police officers, the judge of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court found the applicant guilty of taking part in a meeting on 24 February 2014 which had not been notified to the competent authority in accordance with the procedure provided by law.

At the date of adoption of the present judgment, the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers is continuing its supervision of the pending execution of the judgment in Lashmankin and Others v. Russia (nos. 57818/09 and 14 others, 7 February 2017).

At the 1318th meeting of the Committee of Ministers (June 2018, DH), a decision was adopted (CM/Del/Dec(2018)1318/H46-21) regarding general measures in the execution of the judgment in Lashmankin and Others v. Russia.

The decision adopted at the 1318th meeting of the Committee of Ministers (June 2018) recalled the Council of Europe's readiness, recently expressed by the Secretary General, to assist the Russian Federation in the work to improve its legislation in the field of freedom of assembly.

The decision adopted at the 1318th meeting of the Committee of Ministers (June 2018) noted, as regards judicial practice, a number of positive developments in the form of a series of decisions from the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation over the last years, including an overview of the practice of international bodies and the case-law of the Court concerning freedom of assembly prepared by the Supreme Court.

The decision adopted at the 1318th meeting of the Committee of Ministers (June 2018) noted the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation's ongoing efforts to adopt further guidance to domestic courts on certain issues arising in administrative cases and administrative offences cases regarding the application of the legislation governing the procedure for the organisation and the holding of public events, and encouraged these developments.

The decision adopted at the 1318th meeting of the Committee of Ministers (June 2018) stressed the need to rapidly adopt additional measures, whether in the form of regulations or training and awareness raising measures, to ensure that the practice of relevant municipal authorities and the police, including as regards the use of force, the dispersal of public events and the arrest of participants, is brought into line with the requirements of the Convention.

The decision adopted at the 1318th meeting of the Committee of Ministers (June 2018) highlighted the potential interest of the wide dissemination of the guidelines prepared by the Venice Commission and the OSCE (CDL-AD(2014)046, available also in Russian).
The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights issued a Follow-up Memorandum on Freedom of Assembly in the Russian Federation, dated 5 September 2017.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' Follow-up Memorandum of 5 September 2017 stated that ensuring the safety of participants and public order is a legitimate consideration, but this should not translate into a lack of tolerance towards peaceful public events which have not been agreed with the authorities.
